content.thinking:
I need to examine the legal text and evidence more closely.

Prop 4 repeals the 1988 ban on public campaign funding. It does not create a program itself. State and local governments would establish their own. Funds cannot be used for education, transportation, or public safety.

Public funds must be available to all qualified candidates for the same office without regard to incumbency or party. Candidates must meet strict qualification criteria and abide by expenditure limits. Public money cannot pay legal defense fees, fines, or personal loans.

Strict criteria must require broad-based support, such as small-dollar contributions or resident vouchers. The largest contribution counted may be $10. Candidates cannot be required to collect a specified number of signatures or raise more than $10 per contributor.

A trigger provision for expenditure limits mirrors Arizona's system, which was struck down in Arizona Free Enterprise v. Bennett (2011). The FPPC has no role in local public funding administration or enforcement. Subdivisions (e), (f), and (h) can be amended by simple majority, but other provisions require a two-thirds vote.

The trigger provision caps each candidate's increased expenditure limit at the highest net supportive funds of any other candidate for that office, plus independent expenditures against them, minus independent expenditures in their favor.

The Arizona Free Enterprise ruling likely does not apply here. The trigger provision raises private campaign limits, not public matching funds. Candidates would raise more private money to respond to opponents. This is different from giving extra public money when opponents spend more.

Opponent claims about unlimited candidates and lack of qualification requirements are inaccurate. The text requires candidates to be seeking elective office and to meet strict criteria set by local law. Opponents appear to be quoting an incomplete definition.

Opponents are partially correct that the legislature or local government would set the specific criteria numbers. Those requirements must still mandate broad-based support and cannot require signatures or large fundraising totals. The proposition also does not establish a dollar cap on public funding; future programs would determine those limits.

The proposition does not ban private contributions. Public financing is voluntary and additive. Candidates can still accept private money within program rules. Full public financing would ban private contributions above qualifying amounts. Matching systems allow both public and private funds.

The strongest opponent critique is that local officials who might benefit from the programs could set criteria to favor themselves. The proposition does not require programs to ban private or special interest contributions, so poorly designed systems could allow unlimited private money alongside public funds.

Participation is strictly opt-in. A dedicated fund must be established, and existing earmarked funds for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used.

State programs would require a new statute passed by the legislature. Local programs could be created through ordinance or charter amendment, though charters often require voter approval.

Opponents claim this will reduce funding for schools, public safety, and healthcare. That is misleading. Earmarked funds cannot be redirected, but general fund money could be used instead. The opportunity cost is real.

The LAO estimates implementation costs could be significant if local governments choose to create programs, though the proposition itself only requires a few hundred thousand dollars for FPPC guidance.

Tripling foreign money penalties is a minor side benefit. Current law already bans foreign contributions, and the penalty would increase from equal to three times the amount.

California uniquely bans public campaign financing statewide while exempting charter cities. Evidence from New York, Seattle, Connecticut, Maine, and Washington, D.C. shows that public financing increases small donor participation, candidate diversity, and reduces reliance on large donors.

Good government groups including the League of Women Voters, Common Cause, Clean Money, Consumer Watchdog, and Nurses Association support the proposition. It does not mandate spending. Effects on corruption and policy outcomes are mixed. Citizens United means independent expenditures will continue regardless.

The SF Chronicle's opposition centers on weak guardrails and the FPPC exemption, not a rejection of public financing itself. Oakland's limited program had weak results, confirming that design is critical. Previous voter rejections include Prop 25 in 2000, Prop 89 in 2006, and Prop 15 in 2010.

I am now weighing the final normative judgment. I will check SB 42 history, CalTax arguments, and editorial endorsements from CalMatters and Ballotpedia. I also need to verify whether the $10 qualifying contribution cap is too restrictive and whether amendment provisions weaken protections.

The status quo ban prevents counties and general law cities from testing public financing. Only charter cities can experiment. The measure is permissive rather than mandatory. It preserves choice for voters and governments. The cost of voting yes is option value. The cost of voting no is continued prohibition. Empirical evidence generally supports that well-designed programs improve representation and small-donor participation without the waste opponents claim.

Connecticut's Citizens' Election Program is often cited as a success in reducing corruption. The opponent claims that the proposition offers an unlimited blank check, lacks spending limits, and would fund candidates who do not qualify for the ballot are largely misleading against the actual statutory text.

The FPPC exemption is consistent with existing local campaign finance enforcement and does not undermine the enabling statute. Opponents are primarily taxpayer groups with a categorical objection to using public money for campaigns, rather than design-specific concerns.

The trigger language and amendment provisions could be gamed. Some key definitions can be changed by a simple majority vote. Public financing does not address independent expenditures, the main post-Citizens United problem.

The $10 qualifying contribution cap is a concrete concern. It may force weak qualification standards or require an unreasonably high number of donors. The proposition leaves the exact number unspecified, leaving it to implementers.

The $10 cap could be set to just five donors, trivializing qualification and allowing public funds to flow to fringe candidates. Expenditure limits lack minimum stringency. There is no requirement to restrict private special-interest contributions for participating candidates.

Section (f) allows expenditure limits to increase up to an opponent's net supportive funds. This weakens spending limits against wealthy opponents, though it may help self-funded candidates remain viable. The analysis is now weighing this trade-off in the context of a normative decision.

The ban is the problem being solved, not a specific bad program. The alternative would lock in a system where only wealthy donors and self-funders can compete. Local charter cities already run public financing without the disasters opponents predict. Misleading arguments should not drive the vote. A fiscal conservative perspective favors no. I am now choosing one answer.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
I will examine serious critiques, GAO report findings, McClatchy endorsement reasoning, CalMatters coverage, and potential legal issues with the measure.

The measure is an enabling statute. It does not appropriate campaign money. It repeals a near-total ban and sets minimum conditions for any future public financing program. These include no earmarked education, transportation, or public safety funds. Participation would be voluntary.

The measure also establishes expenditure limits set locally or by statute. It requires broad-based support through small-dollar contributions or vouchers. It prohibits discrimination by party or incumbency. Funds cannot cover legal defense, fines, or personal loan repayment. The FPPC is not required to administer local programs. Foreign money violations face triple maximum fines. Academic literature on public financing is moderately positive but design-sensitive.

Research shows public financing increases candidate numbers and competitiveness. It shifts donor bases toward small, in-district contributors. It may modestly improve legislative effectiveness. It does not eliminate independent expenditures or fully remove wealthy influence. Early partial programs showed weak effects. The GAO found that participating candidates often spend less but win at reasonable rates.

The design critique is valid. The measure does not lock in best-practice parameters like match ratios or independent administration, so future programs could be weak or wasteful.

An enabling measure should not mandate one model because jurisdictions differ and best practices are still evolving. Any actual program would still require a future political act.

Existing charter city programs have operated for years without the apocalyptic outcomes opponents describe. Charter amendments and ordinances are subject to voter approval. A state program would require legislative appropriation. The cost of voting yes is the risk that some jurisdiction designs a weak program. The cost of voting no is that no jurisdiction outside existing charter cities can try public financing.

San Francisco's scandals were caught by local ethics enforcement. Public financing did not create the underlying fraud, and private financing has worse scandals.

Opponent ballot arguments contain false claims. Programs must set strict broad-based support criteria. They do not automatically fund every filing candidate. The measure requires candidates to qualify under program-specific standards.

Opponents also claim the measure imposes no spending limits. It does not specify a statewide cap, though local programs would still set their own. The argument that it allows special interest money is accurate, but California already restricts private contributions through Prop 34.

Public financing is meant to supplement private contributions rather than ban them entirely. Voluntary programs can restrict private money as a condition of participation without violating constitutional principles. New York City's matching program allows private contributions up to limits and is considered the gold standard. The opponent argument treats any private money as a fatal flaw, which would condemn all successful programs.

The measure does not authorize any immediate spending. The LAO estimates only a few hundred thousand dollars annually for FPPC advisory services. Actual program costs would depend on whether local governments opt in, and could be substantial. Seattle's voucher program alone costs roughly three to four million dollars per year.

A statewide program could cost tens of millions, but that is modest relative to the $1 billion spent on state candidate races and the $200 billion general fund. The "$1 per resident" claim falls within typical local program ranges.

The vote splits along familiar lines. Supporters include good-government groups such as the League of Women Voters, Common Cause, Clean Money, and Consumer Watchdog. Opponents are anti-tax organizations like Howard Jarvis and CalTax, plus some former FPPC commissioners.

Editorial board support is mixed. McClatchy, the Sacramento Bee, SPUR, and the Brennan Center recommend yes. The San Francisco Chronicle, Bay Area News Group, and Santa Cruz Sentinel recommend no or are neutral.

Prior rejections addressed specific designs rather than the concept of lifting the ban. Prop 89 proposed a corporate-tax-funded system that voters rejected. Prop 15 was a narrow SOS pilot.

The decision is yes. The policy problem of donor dependence and barriers to entry is real and well-documented.

The remedy is an evidence-based option within constitutional limits after Citizens United. The measure removes an unusual state-wide ban and enables local experimentation. Its safeguards prevent the worst abuses.

I considered whether loose standards would produce incumbent-protecting slush funds or whether budget constraints would make optional authority dangerous. I found these concerns unpersuasive. Incumbents already hold fundraising advantages under the current system. Nondiscriminatory public financing typically benefits challengers more than incumbents.

The nondiscrimination requirement is voter-locked. It can only be amended by a two-thirds vote for furthering PRA purposes. Other provisions, such as definitions and the FPPC exemption, can be changed more easily.

The $10 qualifying contribution cap nudges programs toward small-donor models, which is a best-practice design choice rather than a loophole. The ban on signature requirements as strict criteria prevents petition-based qualification, though it also blocks a potentially useful alternative method.

The enrolled text appears to have dropped the earlier requirement that a dedicated fund be established by statute. Candidates would instead simply abide by expenditure limits and meet strict criteria to qualify for public funds.

The enrolled text still requires a dedicated fund established by statute, ordinance, resolution, or charter. The earlier assumption that this requirement was removed appears incorrect.

The prior text fetch stripped strikeout and italic formatting, so I cannot tell which provisions were deleted or added. I will fetch the leginfo amended law page to see the actual enrolled bill text.

The leginfo text confirms the dedicated fund requirement was removed. The final law now simply prohibits earmarked public funds for education, transportation, or public safety. Candidates must instead abide by expenditure limits and meet strict criteria to qualify for public funds.

Unearmarked public funds may be used, but only after a local government establishes expenditure limits and strict criteria by statute, ordinance, or charter. This requirement is not optional.

Fast Facts
Most electoral campaigns are privately financed. But some states and localities offer programs through which candidates running for state or local offices can use public funds for their campaigns.
We reviewed 5 public financing programs. They all required candidates to collect a specific number of contributions to qualify and then adhere to spending limits.
The average amount of public funding that candidates received varied by office sought. For example, in the 2022 election, mayoral candidates in Los Angeles received about $1.3 million and city council candidates received $198,151.
The average amounts also varied by location.
Skip to Highlights
Highlights
What GAO Found
States and localities have generally implemented public campaign financing programs using one of three models: (1) grants-participating candidates receive lump-sum grants of public funds; (2) matching funds-participating candidates receive public funds matching certain private contributions they raise, at a set rate; and (3) vouchers-eligible residents receive a credit of public funds they can assign to one or more participating candidates. GAO selected five programs representing the three model types (Arizona; Los Angeles, California; Minnesota; Montgomery County, Maryland; and Seattle, Washington) and examined their characteristics. For example, all five programs have requirements for candidates to qualify for the program, and once qualified, to receive public funds. These requirements include, for example, collecting a specific number of contributions to qualify and then adhering to spending limits to receive public funds.
Voting Booths
The amount of public funding participating candidates received varied by office sought and location, among other things. For example, in Minnesota in the 2022 election, legislative candidates received an average of $4,716 in public funds, and the one participating gubernatorial candidate received $584,034 in public funds. In Los Angeles in the 2022 election, participating city council candidates received an average of $198,151 in public funds, and participating mayoral candidates received an average of $1,284,158 in public funds.
GAO interviewed officials from the five selected programs and four additional programs (Albuquerque, New Mexico; Hawaii; Maine; and Washington, D.C.) to obtain perspectives on candidate participation. Officials from all nine programs said that many candidates are attracted to the public campaign financing programs because they provide an accessible source of funding. This may be particularly appealing for candidates with limited fundraising experience. Officials from eight of the nine programs said a key reason candidates may not participate is because they perceive the available public funding to be insufficient to run a competitive campaign.
Why GAO Did This Study
While most electoral campaigns are privately financed, 14 states and 26 localities offer programs through which candidates running for state or local offices can use public funds to finance their campaigns, according to a 2024 Brennan Center for Justice report.
The House committee report accompanying the Financial Services and General Government Appropriations Bill, 2023, includes a provision for GAO to revisit and update its 2010 report ( GAO-10-390 (https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-10-390) ) on public campaign financing programs. This report describes, among other things, (1) key characteristics of public campaign financing programs in selected states and localities; (2) what available data indicate about candidates' use of these programs; and (3) factors affecting candidate participation in these programs.
GAO selected five locations with state and local public campaign financing programs that covered executive and legislative offices, were implemented for at least two election cycles, and represented a mix of program models, among other factors. GAO reviewed relevant laws and documents and interviewed officials to describe key characteristics of the selected programs. GAO also analyzed candidate participation and campaign finance data for these five programs for the two most recent election cycles.
GAO interviewed officials from these five programs and four additional programs-selected using the same criteria-to obtain perspectives on public campaign financing programs. The findings from these interviews are not generalizable, but provide insight into state and local perspectives.

McClatchy Media’s endorsements for all 14 propositions on California’s ballot
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
Updated October 27, 2026 9:16 AM
The California state Capitol on Aug. 31, 2026.
Lauren Chapman
lchapman@sacbee.com
Opinion journalists for McClatchy Media conducted interviews with supporters and opponents of all 14 statewide propositions on your November ballot. The journalists then deliberated and decided how they would vote on each one, just as voters do. Their endorsements, linked below, explain their positions.
What to Know
Here are key takeaways:
Prop. 1 would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds for affordable housing and CalVet home loans (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317326136.html#storylink=var-wtk), with $10 billion aimed at closing financing gaps for nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes already in the pipeline. The board endorsed a “yes” vote but urged the state to publish a transparent dashboard tracking costs and results.
Prop. 2 would raise California’s rainy day fund cap from 10% to 20% (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317091637.html#storylink=var-wtk) of annual tax collections and allow some reserves to pay down state debts, including $20 billion still owed to the federal government for pandemic-era unemployment borrowing. The board recommended a “yes” vote as a safeguard against future downturns.
Prop. 3 would make permanent a tax on California’s top 2% of earners (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317445836.html#storylink=var-wtk) — single filers making at least $361,000 and joint filers at least $721,000 — that generates between $5 billion and $15 billion a year for schools and community colleges. The board endorsed a “yes” vote.
Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on public financing of state and local campaigns (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317448027.html#storylink=var-wtk), allowing matching-fund or public-grant programs for qualifying candidates. The board backed a “yes” vote, arguing public financing reduces reliance on wealthy donors.
Prop. 5 would eliminate the second question on recall ballots asking who should replace an ousted official (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316911387.html#storylink=var-wtk), instead triggering special elections or gubernatorial appointments. The board strongly endorsed a “yes” vote, noting past recalls have installed replacements with less voter support than the official removed.
Prop. 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to finance second mortgages (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317470188.html#storylink=var-wtk) covering up to 17% of a new home’s price for middle-class buyers. Despite reservations about default risk, the board recommended a “yes” vote.
Prop. 38 proposes an $8.4 billion bond for immunology research (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166634.html#storylink=var-wtk), with half guaranteed to an institute tied to UCLA and backed by billionaire physician Gary K. Michelson. The board urged a “no” vote, warning the measure would exempt the institute from public-records laws.
Prop. 39 would require government-issued ID at the polls and partial ID numbers on mail ballots (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317017898.html#storylink=var-wtk), with backers including nine billionaires tracked by Forbes. The board recommended a “no” vote, warning the measure would disenfranchise more legitimate voters than it would stop fraudulent ones.
Prop. 40 would impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on Californians worth more than $1 billion (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317269166.html#storylink=var-wtk), with 90% of proceeds reserved for healthcare amid federal Medi-Cal cuts projected to cost 1.3 million residents coverage by 2030. A majority of the board endorsed a “yes” vote.
Prop. 41 is a constitutional amendment backed by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other wealthy donors that would ban taxes exempt from state spending limits on or after Jan. 1, 2026 (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html#storylink=var-wtk) — a provision that could nullify Prop. 40. The board urged a “no” vote.
Prop. 42 is billed as a safeguard for 401(k) accounts and personal property, but the board called it a “poison pill” designed to derail the billionaire wealth tax (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166989.html#storylink=var-wtk) in Prop. 40. If Prop. 42 gets more yes votes than Prop. 40, Prop. 40 would not take effect. Vote “no,” the board said.
Prop. 43 would raise the threshold to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives from a simple majority to 66.7% (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316956235.html#storylink=var-wtk), giving a 33.3% minority the power to block measures funding fire, police, flood control and other local services. The board opposed it and urged a “no” vote.
Prop. 44, the Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act, would require federally qualified health centers to spend at least 90% of revenue on patient services (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317472706.html#storylink=var-wtk), up from the roughly 80% most currently report. The board recommended a “no” vote, citing warnings the mandate could force clinics serving nearly 7 million patients to close.
Prop. 45 would reshape the California Environmental Quality Act (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317475362.html#storylink=var-wtk) by tightening deadlines, limiting public-comment periods and barring judges from halting entire projects over partial violations. The board endorsed a “yes” vote, arguing CEQA has too often been used to block needed housing.
The summary points above were compiled with the help of AI tools and edited by journalists. The source reporting referenced above was written and edited entirely by journalists.

Fast Facts
Most electoral campaigns are privately financed. But some states and localities offer programs through which candidates running for state or local offices can use public funds for their campaigns.
We reviewed 5 public financing programs. They all required candidates to collect a specific number of contributions to qualify and then adhere to spending limits.
The average amount of public funding that candidates received varied by office sought. For example, in the 2022 election, mayoral candidates in Los Angeles received about $1.3 million and city council candidates received $198,151.
The average amounts also varied by location.
Skip to Highlights
Highlights
What GAO Found
States and localities have generally implemented public campaign financing programs using one of three models: (1) grants-participating candidates receive lump-sum grants of public funds; (2) matching funds-participating candidates receive public funds matching certain private contributions they raise, at a set rate; and (3) vouchers-eligible residents receive a credit of public funds they can assign to one or more participating candidates. GAO selected five programs representing the three model types (Arizona; Los Angeles, California; Minnesota; Montgomery County, Maryland; and Seattle, Washington) and examined their characteristics. For example, all five programs have requirements for candidates to qualify for the program, and once qualified, to receive public funds. These requirements include, for example, collecting a specific number of contributions to qualify and then adhering to spending limits to receive public funds.
Voting Booths
The amount of public funding participating candidates received varied by office sought and location, among other things. For example, in Minnesota in the 2022 election, legislative candidates received an average of $4,716 in public funds, and the one participating gubernatorial candidate received $584,034 in public funds. In Los Angeles in the 2022 election, participating city council candidates received an average of $198,151 in public funds, and participating mayoral candidates received an average of $1,284,158 in public funds.
GAO interviewed officials from the five selected programs and four additional programs (Albuquerque, New Mexico; Hawaii; Maine; and Washington, D.C.) to obtain perspectives on candidate participation. Officials from all nine programs said that many candidates are attracted to the public campaign financing programs because they provide an accessible source of funding. This may be particularly appealing for candidates with limited fundraising experience. Officials from eight of the nine programs said a key reason candidates may not participate is because they perceive the available public funding to be insufficient to run a competitive campaign.
Why GAO Did This Study
While most electoral campaigns are privately financed, 14 states and 26 localities offer programs through which candidates running for state or local offices can use public funds to finance their campaigns, according to a 2024 Brennan Center for Justice report.
The House committee report accompanying the Financial Services and General Government Appropriations Bill, 2023, includes a provision for GAO to revisit and update its 2010 report ( GAO-10-390 (https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-10-390) ) on public campaign financing programs. This report describes, among other things, (1) key characteristics of public campaign financing programs in selected states and localities; (2) what available data indicate about candidates' use of these programs; and (3) factors affecting candidate participation in these programs.
GAO selected five locations with state and local public campaign financing programs that covered executive and legislative offices, were implemented for at least two election cycles, and represented a mix of program models, among other factors. GAO reviewed relevant laws and documents and interviewed officials to describe key characteristics of the selected programs. GAO also analyzed candidate participation and campaign finance data for these five programs for the two most recent election cycles.
GAO interviewed officials from these five programs and four additional programs-selected using the same criteria-to obtain perspectives on public campaign financing programs. The findings from these interviews are not generalizable, but provide insight into state and local perspectives.

Fast Facts
Most electoral campaigns are privately financed. But some states and localities offer programs through which candidates running for state or local offices can use public funds for their campaigns.
We reviewed 5 public financing programs. They all required candidates to collect a specific number of contributions to qualify and then adhere to spending limits.
The average amount of public funding that candidates received varied by office sought. For example, in the 2022 election, mayoral candidates in Los Angeles received about $1.3 million and city council candidates received $198,151.
The average amounts also varied by location.
Skip to Highlights
Highlights
What GAO Found
States and localities have generally implemented public campaign financing programs using one of three models: (1) grants-participating candidates receive lump-sum grants of public funds; (2) matching funds-participating candidates receive public funds matching certain private contributions they raise, at a set rate; and (3) vouchers-eligible residents receive a credit of public funds they can assign to one or more participating candidates. GAO selected five programs representing the three model types (Arizona; Los Angeles, California; Minnesota; Montgomery County, Maryland; and Seattle, Washington) and examined their characteristics. For example, all five programs have requirements for candidates to qualify for the program, and once qualified, to receive public funds. These requirements include, for example, collecting a specific number of contributions to qualify and then adhering to spending limits to receive public funds.
Voting Booths
The amount of public funding participating candidates received varied by office sought and location, among other things. For example, in Minnesota in the 2022 election, legislative candidates received an average of $4,716 in public funds, and the one participating gubernatorial candidate received $584,034 in public funds. In Los Angeles in the 2022 election, participating city council candidates received an average of $198,151 in public funds, and participating mayoral candidates received an average of $1,284,158 in public funds.
GAO interviewed officials from the five selected programs and four additional programs (Albuquerque, New Mexico; Hawaii; Maine; and Washington, D.C.) to obtain perspectives on candidate participation. Officials from all nine programs said that many candidates are attracted to the public campaign financing programs because they provide an accessible source of funding. This may be particularly appealing for candidates with limited fundraising experience. Officials from eight of the nine programs said a key reason candidates may not participate is because they perceive the available public funding to be insufficient to run a competitive campaign.
Why GAO Did This Study
While most electoral campaigns are privately financed, 14 states and 26 localities offer programs through which candidates running for state or local offices can use public funds to finance their campaigns, according to a 2024 Brennan Center for Justice report.
The House committee report accompanying the Financial Services and General Government Appropriations Bill, 2023, includes a provision for GAO to revisit and update its 2010 report ( GAO-10-390 (https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-10-390) ) on public campaign financing programs. This report describes, among other things, (1) key characteristics of public campaign financing programs in selected states and localities; (2) what available data indicate about candidates' use of these programs; and (3) factors affecting candidate participation in these programs.
GAO selected five locations with state and local public campaign financing programs that covered executive and legislative offices, were implemented for at least two election cycles, and represented a mix of program models, among other factors. GAO reviewed relevant laws and documents and interviewed officials to describe key characteristics of the selected programs. GAO also analyzed candidate participation and campaign finance data for these five programs for the two most recent election cycles.
GAO interviewed officials from these five programs and four additional programs-selected using the same criteria-to obtain perspectives on public campaign financing programs. The findings from these interviews are not generalizable, but provide insight into state and local perspectives.

McClatchy Media’s endorsements for all 14 propositions on California’s ballot
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
Updated October 27, 2026 9:16 AM
The California state Capitol on Aug. 31, 2026.
Lauren Chapman
lchapman@sacbee.com
Opinion journalists for McClatchy Media conducted interviews with supporters and opponents of all 14 statewide propositions on your November ballot. The journalists then deliberated and decided how they would vote on each one, just as voters do. Their endorsements, linked below, explain their positions.
What to Know
Here are key takeaways:
Prop. 1 would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds for affordable housing and CalVet home loans (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317326136.html#storylink=var-wtk), with $10 billion aimed at closing financing gaps for nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes already in the pipeline. The board endorsed a “yes” vote but urged the state to publish a transparent dashboard tracking costs and results.
Prop. 2 would raise California’s rainy day fund cap from 10% to 20% (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317091637.html#storylink=var-wtk) of annual tax collections and allow some reserves to pay down state debts, including $20 billion still owed to the federal government for pandemic-era unemployment borrowing. The board recommended a “yes” vote as a safeguard against future downturns.
Prop. 3 would make permanent a tax on California’s top 2% of earners (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317445836.html#storylink=var-wtk) — single filers making at least $361,000 and joint filers at least $721,000 — that generates between $5 billion and $15 billion a year for schools and community colleges. The board endorsed a “yes” vote.
Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on public financing of state and local campaigns (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317448027.html#storylink=var-wtk), allowing matching-fund or public-grant programs for qualifying candidates. The board backed a “yes” vote, arguing public financing reduces reliance on wealthy donors.
Prop. 5 would eliminate the second question on recall ballots asking who should replace an ousted official (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316911387.html#storylink=var-wtk), instead triggering special elections or gubernatorial appointments. The board strongly endorsed a “yes” vote, noting past recalls have installed replacements with less voter support than the official removed.
Prop. 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to finance second mortgages (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317470188.html#storylink=var-wtk) covering up to 17% of a new home’s price for middle-class buyers. Despite reservations about default risk, the board recommended a “yes” vote.
Prop. 38 proposes an $8.4 billion bond for immunology research (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166634.html#storylink=var-wtk), with half guaranteed to an institute tied to UCLA and backed by billionaire physician Gary K. Michelson. The board urged a “no” vote, warning the measure would exempt the institute from public-records laws.
Prop. 39 would require government-issued ID at the polls and partial ID numbers on mail ballots (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317017898.html#storylink=var-wtk), with backers including nine billionaires tracked by Forbes. The board recommended a “no” vote, warning the measure would disenfranchise more legitimate voters than it would stop fraudulent ones.
Prop. 40 would impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on Californians worth more than $1 billion (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317269166.html#storylink=var-wtk), with 90% of proceeds reserved for healthcare amid federal Medi-Cal cuts projected to cost 1.3 million residents coverage by 2030. A majority of the board endorsed a “yes” vote.
Prop. 41 is a constitutional amendment backed by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other wealthy donors that would ban taxes exempt from state spending limits on or after Jan. 1, 2026 (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html#storylink=var-wtk) — a provision that could nullify Prop. 40. The board urged a “no” vote.
Prop. 42 is billed as a safeguard for 401(k) accounts and personal property, but the board called it a “poison pill” designed to derail the billionaire wealth tax (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166989.html#storylink=var-wtk) in Prop. 40. If Prop. 42 gets more yes votes than Prop. 40, Prop. 40 would not take effect. Vote “no,” the board said.
Prop. 43 would raise the threshold to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives from a simple majority to 66.7% (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316956235.html#storylink=var-wtk), giving a 33.3% minority the power to block measures funding fire, police, flood control and other local services. The board opposed it and urged a “no” vote.
Prop. 44, the Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act, would require federally qualified health centers to spend at least 90% of revenue on patient services (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317472706.html#storylink=var-wtk), up from the roughly 80% most currently report. The board recommended a “no” vote, citing warnings the mandate could force clinics serving nearly 7 million patients to close.
Prop. 45 would reshape the California Environmental Quality Act (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317475362.html#storylink=var-wtk) by tightening deadlines, limiting public-comment periods and barring judges from halting entire projects over partial violations. The board endorsed a “yes” vote, arguing CEQA has too often been used to block needed housing.
The summary points above were compiled with the help of AI tools and edited by journalists. The source reporting referenced above was written and edited entirely by journalists.

Prop. 1 would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds for affordable housing and CalVet home loans (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317326136.html#storylink=var-wtk), with $10 billion aimed at closing financing gaps for nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes already in the pipeline. The board endorsed a “yes” vote but urged the state to publish a transparent dashboard tracking costs and results.
Prop. 2 would raise California’s rainy day fund cap from 10% to 20% (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317091637.html#storylink=var-wtk) of annual tax collections and allow some reserves to pay down state debts, including $20 billion still owed to the federal government for pandemic-era unemployment borrowing. The board recommended a “yes” vote as a safeguard against future downturns.
Prop. 3 would make permanent a tax on California’s top 2% of earners (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317445836.html#storylink=var-wtk) — single filers making at least $361,000 and joint filers at least $721,000 — that generates between $5 billion and $15 billion a year for schools and community colleges. The board endorsed a “yes” vote.
Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on public financing of state and local campaigns (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317448027.html#storylink=var-wtk), allowing matching-fund or public-grant programs for qualifying candidates. The board backed a “yes” vote, arguing public financing reduces reliance on wealthy donors.
Prop. 5 would eliminate the second question on recall ballots asking who should replace an ousted official (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316911387.html#storylink=var-wtk), instead triggering special elections or gubernatorial appointments. The board strongly endorsed a “yes” vote, noting past recalls have installed replacements with less voter support than the official removed.
Prop. 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to finance second mortgages (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317470188.html#storylink=var-wtk) covering up to 17% of a new home’s price for middle-class buyers. Despite reservations about default risk, the board recommended a “yes” vote.
Prop. 38 proposes an $8.4 billion bond for immunology research (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166634.html#storylink=var-wtk), with half guaranteed to an institute tied to UCLA and backed by billionaire physician Gary K. Michelson. The board urged a “no” vote, warning the measure would exempt the institute from public-records laws.
Prop. 39 would require government-issued ID at the polls and partial ID numbers on mail ballots (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317017898.html#storylink=var-wtk), with backers including nine billionaires tracked by Forbes. The board recommended a “no” vote, warning the measure would disenfranchise more legitimate voters than it would stop fraudulent ones.
Prop. 40 would impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on Californians worth more than $1 billion (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317269166.html#storylink=var-wtk), with 90% of proceeds reserved for healthcare amid federal Medi-Cal cuts projected to cost 1.3 million residents coverage by 2030. A majority of the board endorsed a “yes” vote.
Prop. 41 is a constitutional amendment backed by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other wealthy donors that would ban taxes exempt from state spending limits on or after Jan. 1, 2026 (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html#storylink=var-wtk) — a provision that could nullify Prop. 40. The board urged a “no” vote.
Prop. 42 is billed as a safeguard for 401(k) accounts and personal property, but the board called it a “poison pill” designed to derail the billionaire wealth tax (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166989.html#storylink=var-wtk) in Prop. 40. If Prop. 42 gets more yes votes than Prop. 40, Prop. 40 would not take effect. Vote “no,” the board said.
Prop. 43 would raise the threshold to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives from a simple majority to 66.7% (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316956235.html#storylink=var-wtk), giving a 33.3% minority the power to block measures funding fire, police, flood control and other local services. The board opposed it and urged a “no” vote.
Prop. 44, the Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act, would require federally qualified health centers to spend at least 90% of revenue on patient services (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317472706.html#storylink=var-wtk), up from the roughly 80% most currently report. The board recommended a “no” vote, citing warnings the mandate could force clinics serving nearly 7 million patients to close.
Prop. 45 would reshape the California Environmental Quality Act (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317475362.html#storylink=var-wtk) by tightening deadlines, limiting public-comment periods and barring judges from halting entire projects over partial violations. The board endorsed a “yes” vote, arguing CEQA has too often been used to block needed housing.

I will examine serious critiques, GAO report findings, McClatchy endorsement reasoning, CalMatters coverage, and potential legal issues with the measure.

The measure is an enabling statute. It does not appropriate campaign money. It repeals a near-total ban and sets minimum conditions for any future public financing program. These include no earmarked education, transportation, or public safety funds. Participation would be voluntary.

The measure also establishes expenditure limits set locally or by statute. It requires broad-based support through small-dollar contributions or vouchers. It prohibits discrimination by party or incumbency. Funds cannot cover legal defense, fines, or personal loan repayment. The FPPC is not required to administer local programs. Foreign money violations face triple maximum fines. Academic literature on public financing is moderately positive but design-sensitive.

Research shows public financing increases candidate numbers and competitiveness. It shifts donor bases toward small, in-district contributors. It may modestly improve legislative effectiveness. It does not eliminate independent expenditures or fully remove wealthy influence. Early partial programs showed weak effects. The GAO found that participating candidates often spend less but win at reasonable rates.

The design critique is valid. The measure does not lock in best-practice parameters like match ratios or independent administration, so future programs could be weak or wasteful.

An enabling measure should not mandate one model because jurisdictions differ and best practices are still evolving. Any actual program would still require a future political act.

Existing charter city programs have operated for years without the apocalyptic outcomes opponents describe. Charter amendments and ordinances are subject to voter approval. A state program would require legislative appropriation. The cost of voting yes is the risk that some jurisdiction designs a weak program. The cost of voting no is that no jurisdiction outside existing charter cities can try public financing.

San Francisco's scandals were caught by local ethics enforcement. Public financing did not create the underlying fraud, and private financing has worse scandals.

Opponent ballot arguments contain false claims. Programs must set strict broad-based support criteria. They do not automatically fund every filing candidate. The measure requires candidates to qualify under program-specific standards.

Opponents also claim the measure imposes no spending limits. It does not specify a statewide cap, though local programs would still set their own. The argument that it allows special interest money is accurate, but California already restricts private contributions through Prop 34.

Public financing is meant to supplement private contributions rather than ban them entirely. Voluntary programs can restrict private money as a condition of participation without violating constitutional principles. New York City's matching program allows private contributions up to limits and is considered the gold standard. The opponent argument treats any private money as a fatal flaw, which would condemn all successful programs.

The measure does not authorize any immediate spending. The LAO estimates only a few hundred thousand dollars annually for FPPC advisory services. Actual program costs would depend on whether local governments opt in, and could be substantial. Seattle's voucher program alone costs roughly three to four million dollars per year.

A statewide program could cost tens of millions, but that is modest relative to the $1 billion spent on state candidate races and the $200 billion general fund. The "$1 per resident" claim falls within typical local program ranges.

The vote splits along familiar lines. Supporters include good-government groups such as the League of Women Voters, Common Cause, Clean Money, and Consumer Watchdog. Opponents are anti-tax organizations like Howard Jarvis and CalTax, plus some former FPPC commissioners.

Editorial board support is mixed. McClatchy, the Sacramento Bee, SPUR, and the Brennan Center recommend yes. The San Francisco Chronicle, Bay Area News Group, and Santa Cruz Sentinel recommend no or are neutral.

Prior rejections addressed specific designs rather than the concept of lifting the ban. Prop 89 proposed a corporate-tax-funded system that voters rejected. Prop 15 was a narrow SOS pilot.

The decision is yes. The policy problem of donor dependence and barriers to entry is real and well-documented.

The remedy is an evidence-based option within constitutional limits after Citizens United. The measure removes an unusual state-wide ban and enables local experimentation. Its safeguards prevent the worst abuses.

I considered whether loose standards would produce incumbent-protecting slush funds or whether budget constraints would make optional authority dangerous. I found these concerns unpersuasive. Incumbents already hold fundraising advantages under the current system. Nondiscriminatory public financing typically benefits challengers more than incumbents.

The nondiscrimination requirement is voter-locked. It can only be amended by a two-thirds vote for furthering PRA purposes. Other provisions, such as definitions and the FPPC exemption, can be changed more easily.

The $10 qualifying contribution cap nudges programs toward small-donor models, which is a best-practice design choice rather than a loophole. The ban on signature requirements as strict criteria prevents petition-based qualification, though it also blocks a potentially useful alternative method.

The enrolled text appears to have dropped the earlier requirement that a dedicated fund be established by statute. Candidates would instead simply abide by expenditure limits and meet strict criteria to qualify for public funds.

The enrolled text still requires a dedicated fund established by statute, ordinance, resolution, or charter. The earlier assumption that this requirement was removed appears incorrect.

The prior text fetch stripped strikeout and italic formatting, so I cannot tell which provisions were deleted or added. I will fetch the leginfo amended law page to see the actual enrolled bill text.

The leginfo text confirms the dedicated fund requirement was removed. The final law now simply prohibits earmarked public funds for education, transportation, or public safety. Candidates must instead abide by expenditure limits and meet strict criteria to qualify for public funds.

Unearmarked public funds may be used, but only after a local government establishes expenditure limits and strict criteria by statute, ordinance, or charter. This requirement is not optional.

Fast Facts
Most electoral campaigns are privately financed. But some states and localities offer programs through which candidates running for state or local offices can use public funds for their campaigns.
We reviewed 5 public financing programs. They all required candidates to collect a specific number of contributions to qualify and then adhere to spending limits.
The average amount of public funding that candidates received varied by office sought. For example, in the 2022 election, mayoral candidates in Los Angeles received about $1.3 million and city council candidates received $198,151.
The average amounts also varied by location.
Skip to Highlights
Highlights
What GAO Found
States and localities have generally implemented public campaign financing programs using one of three models: (1) grants-participating candidates receive lump-sum grants of public funds; (2) matching funds-participating candidates receive public funds matching certain private contributions they raise, at a set rate; and (3) vouchers-eligible residents receive a credit of public funds they can assign to one or more participating candidates. GAO selected five programs representing the three model types (Arizona; Los Angeles, California; Minnesota; Montgomery County, Maryland; and Seattle, Washington) and examined their characteristics. For example, all five programs have requirements for candidates to qualify for the program, and once qualified, to receive public funds. These requirements include, for example, collecting a specific number of contributions to qualify and then adhering to spending limits to receive public funds.
Voting Booths
The amount of public funding participating candidates received varied by office sought and location, among other things. For example, in Minnesota in the 2022 election, legislative candidates received an average of $4,716 in public funds, and the one participating gubernatorial candidate received $584,034 in public funds. In Los Angeles in the 2022 election, participating city council candidates received an average of $198,151 in public funds, and participating mayoral candidates received an average of $1,284,158 in public funds.
GAO interviewed officials from the five selected programs and four additional programs (Albuquerque, New Mexico; Hawaii; Maine; and Washington, D.C.) to obtain perspectives on candidate participation. Officials from all nine programs said that many candidates are attracted to the public campaign financing programs because they provide an accessible source of funding. This may be particularly appealing for candidates with limited fundraising experience. Officials from eight of the nine programs said a key reason candidates may not participate is because they perceive the available public funding to be insufficient to run a competitive campaign.
Why GAO Did This Study
While most electoral campaigns are privately financed, 14 states and 26 localities offer programs through which candidates running for state or local offices can use public funds to finance their campaigns, according to a 2024 Brennan Center for Justice report.
The House committee report accompanying the Financial Services and General Government Appropriations Bill, 2023, includes a provision for GAO to revisit and update its 2010 report ( GAO-10-390 (https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-10-390) ) on public campaign financing programs. This report describes, among other things, (1) key characteristics of public campaign financing programs in selected states and localities; (2) what available data indicate about candidates' use of these programs; and (3) factors affecting candidate participation in these programs.
GAO selected five locations with state and local public campaign financing programs that covered executive and legislative offices, were implemented for at least two election cycles, and represented a mix of program models, among other factors. GAO reviewed relevant laws and documents and interviewed officials to describe key characteristics of the selected programs. GAO also analyzed candidate participation and campaign finance data for these five programs for the two most recent election cycles.
GAO interviewed officials from these five programs and four additional programs-selected using the same criteria-to obtain perspectives on public campaign financing programs. The findings from these interviews are not generalizable, but provide insight into state and local perspectives.
For more information, contact Rebecca Gambler at (202) 512-8777 or gamblerr@gao.gov (mailto:gamblerr@gao.gov).

McClatchy Media’s endorsements for all 14 propositions on California’s ballot
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial boards
Updated October 27, 2026 9:16 AM
The California state Capitol on Aug. 31, 2026.
Lauren Chapman
lchapman@sacbee.com
Opinion journalists for McClatchy Media conducted interviews with supporters and opponents of all 14 statewide propositions on your November ballot. The journalists then deliberated and decided how they would vote on each one, just as voters do. Their endorsements, linked below, explain their positions.
What to Know
Here are key takeaways:
Prop. 1 would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds for affordable housing and CalVet home loans (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317326136.html#storylink=var-wtk), with $10 billion aimed at closing financing gaps for nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes already in the pipeline. The board endorsed a “yes” vote but urged the state to publish a transparent dashboard tracking costs and results.
Prop. 2 would raise California’s rainy day fund cap from 10% to 20% (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317091637.html#storylink=var-wtk) of annual tax collections and allow some reserves to pay down state debts, including $20 billion still owed to the federal government for pandemic-era unemployment borrowing. The board recommended a “yes” vote as a safeguard against future downturns.
Prop. 3 would make permanent a tax on California’s top 2% of earners (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317445836.html#storylink=var-wtk) — single filers making at least $361,000 and joint filers at least $721,000 — that generates between $5 billion and $15 billion a year for schools and community colleges. The board endorsed a “yes” vote.
Prop. 4 would repeal a more than 30-year ban on public financing of state and local campaigns (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317448027.html#storylink=var-wtk), allowing matching-fund or public-grant programs for qualifying candidates. The board backed a “yes” vote, arguing public financing reduces reliance on wealthy donors.
Prop. 5 would eliminate the second question on recall ballots asking who should replace an ousted official (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316911387.html#storylink=var-wtk), instead triggering special elections or gubernatorial appointments. The board strongly endorsed a “yes” vote, noting past recalls have installed replacements with less voter support than the official removed.
Prop. 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to finance second mortgages (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317470188.html#storylink=var-wtk) covering up to 17% of a new home’s price for middle-class buyers. Despite reservations about default risk, the board recommended a “yes” vote.
Prop. 38 proposes an $8.4 billion bond for immunology research (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166634.html#storylink=var-wtk), with half guaranteed to an institute tied to UCLA and backed by billionaire physician Gary K. Michelson. The board urged a “no” vote, warning the measure would exempt the institute from public-records laws.
Prop. 39 would require government-issued ID at the polls and partial ID numbers on mail ballots (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317017898.html#storylink=var-wtk), with backers including nine billionaires tracked by Forbes. The board recommended a “no” vote, warning the measure would disenfranchise more legitimate voters than it would stop fraudulent ones.
Prop. 40 would impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on Californians worth more than $1 billion (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317269166.html#storylink=var-wtk), with 90% of proceeds reserved for healthcare amid federal Medi-Cal cuts projected to cost 1.3 million residents coverage by 2030. A majority of the board endorsed a “yes” vote.
Prop. 41 is a constitutional amendment backed by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other wealthy donors that would ban taxes exempt from state spending limits on or after Jan. 1, 2026 (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html#storylink=var-wtk) — a provision that could nullify Prop. 40. The board urged a “no” vote.
Prop. 42 is billed as a safeguard for 401(k) accounts and personal property, but the board called it a “poison pill” designed to derail the billionaire wealth tax (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166989.html#storylink=var-wtk) in Prop. 40. If Prop. 42 gets more yes votes than Prop. 40, Prop. 40 would not take effect. Vote “no,” the board said.
Prop. 43 would raise the threshold to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives from a simple majority to 66.7% (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316956235.html#storylink=var-wtk), giving a 33.3% minority the power to block measures funding fire, police, flood control and other local services. The board opposed it and urged a “no” vote.
Prop. 44, the Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act, would require federally qualified health centers to spend at least 90% of revenue on patient services (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317472706.html#storylink=var-wtk), up from the roughly 80% most currently report. The board recommended a “no” vote, citing warnings the mandate could force clinics serving nearly 7 million patients to close.
Prop. 45 would reshape the California Environmental Quality Act (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317475362.html#storylink=var-wtk) by tightening deadlines, limiting public-comment periods and barring judges from halting entire projects over partial violations. The board endorsed a “yes” vote, arguing CEQA has too often been used to block needed housing.
The summary points above were compiled with the help of AI tools and edited by journalists. The source reporting referenced above was written and edited entirely by journalists.

Should California taxpayers chip in to fund political campaigns? Prop. 4 lets you decide
by
Yue Stella Yu (https://calmatters.org/author/yue-yu/)
October 15, 2026 Updated November 2, 2026

Steyer poses for a photo with students during a Get the Youth Vote event with Bruin Democrats at UCLA in Los Angeles on June 1, 2026. Photo by Mario Tama, Getty Images
In summary
Prop. 4 would lift a ban that prohibits state and most local candidates from using public funding for their political campaigns. Proponents argue the mechanism helps more candidates run for office, but opponents are skeptical.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
In 1988, a Democrat, a Republican and an independent in the state Legislature co-authored a ballot measure to ban most political campaigns from using public money.
Their rationale? There was already too much money in politics.
“It certainly makes no sense to open the biggest money source of all, the taxpayers’ purses and wallets,” proponents argued (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1988&context=ca_ballot_props). Nearly 60% of voters agreed.
Almost four decades later, some good-government groups argue that the state needs to do the exact opposite to counter the influence of money in politics.
They, along with the state Democratic Party, are backing Proposition 4 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-4-public-fundraising/) on the November ballot, which would lift the 1988 ban and authorize the state and most local governments to set up public campaign financing systems for state and local races.
Seven charter cities in California, including San Francisco, Berkeley and Oakland, were spared from the 1988 ban and already have public campaign financing.
To qualify for the funding, candidates must meet criteria such as proving they have a certain number of small donors or agreeing to cap how much they raise and spend on their campaign. Depending on the city, eligible candidates receive the funding as a grant, a matching fund indexed to their total donations, or a voucher voters can give to campaigns.
Proponents of Prop. 4 may face an uphill battle: Voters have twice rejected similar ballot measures to lift the ban, and public polling so far suggests voters are skeptical.
What supporters, opponents say
Elections have gotten more expensive over the past three decades, both federally and statewide.
In 2000, federal candidates, parties and special interests spent $5.6 billion on congressional and presidential races. By 2020, that number had nearly quadrupled to $18 billion (https://www.opensecrets.org/elections-overview/cost-of-election?display=T), according to OpenSecrets, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit that tracks campaign spending nationwide.
In California, special interests spent $26 million (https://calmatters.org/politics/2025/10/prop50-money-ads-mailers-billboards/) running competing ads on redistricting last year, making it the most expensive ballot measure race in state history. This year, California had the most expensive governor’s race (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/03/us/elections/california-governor-campaign-finance.html) in U.S. history, with billionaire Tom Steyer pouring $213 million (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-rich-candidates-funding-elections/) of his own money into his unsuccessful gubernatorial bid.
Supporters of Prop. 4 say public campaign financing is necessary as a check against that kind of unfettered private campaign spending, because candidates often must accept campaign spending limits to qualify for public funding. They say public financing will lead to more diverse candidates by attracting those who otherwise couldn’t afford to run for office.

“We need to change the way we finance election campaigns so candidates can run and win without having to raise big money, and they can spend their time listening to voters rather than their donors,” said Trent Lange, president of California Clean Money Campaign and co-chair of the Yes on Prop. 4 campaign.
Gov. Gavin Newsom (https://calmatters.org/tag/gavin-newsom/) and the Democratic-led state Legislature, which voted last year (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb42) to place Prop. 4 on the November ballot, also support the measure. Sen. Tom Umberg (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/thomas-umberg-165043), a Santa Ana Democrat and a co-author of Prop. 4, said it would help alleviate a “growing cynicism in politics” and allow candidates to spend more time developing policies instead of fundraising.
“To the extent that we can engage particularly small donors, that will … empower and also engage the body politic, particularly young people,” he said.
But opponents say politicians should not use taxpayer dollars (https://caltax.org/prop4/) to run campaigns. They argue the measure would force voters to subsidize candidates they otherwise wouldn’t support, and that fraudulent candidates could exploit the system.
Voters have previously rejected ballot initiatives that would have allowed public money to be used for political campaigns. Nearly two-thirds of voters shot down a 2000 measure that would have allowed candidates to tap public funds for advertising (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2000/25_03_2000.html). In 2010, 58% of voters opposed a 2010 measure (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_15,_Biennial_Lobbyist_Fee_and_Public_Campaign_Funding_Measure_(June_2010)) to lift the 1988 ban.
“The voters have been quite clear they don’t want taxpayer money being used for politics,” Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican, said last year (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/278290#t=221&f=fe479f37ee7a3df6888379e9be069fd8) on the Assembly floor. “Unfortunately, politicians simply can’t take no for an answer.”

Critics also doubt the effectiveness of Prop. 4, arguing it is not specific enough to have teeth.
Prop. 4 offers only broad instructions to local governments and the state. It would ban candidates from using public funds meant for education, public safety and transportation. It would require candidates to prove they have enough public support and to agree to certain spending limits to receive funding, but doesn’t spell out how much. It would also ban candidates from using the money to pay for legal defenses, fines or personal loans to their campaigns.
The measure specifically exempts the Fair Political Practices Commission, the state’s campaign finance watchdog, from ensuring local programs are not exploited or abused, leaving it largely to local governments. But not every local government has its own watchdog agency, let alone an effective one.
The San Francisco Chronicle’s editorial board, in opposing Prop. 4, argued that its rules “are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop. 4 offers no guarantee they will be.”
Effectiveness debate
Fifteen states and Washington, D.C., offer some sort of statewide public financing for political campaigns, according to an analysis by the National Conference of State Legislatures (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/public-financing-of-campaigns-overview).
Studies are mixed on the effectiveness of those programs.
Some, including one in 2003 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1532673X03256784) by two University of Maryland scholars, suggest that candidates who accept public financing spend less time fundraising, freeing them up for other campaign activities.
Some researchers found that public financing expanded the pool of candidates running for office. A 2022 study of Seattle’s program (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0047272722000780), which gives each registered voter four $25 vouchers to contribute to the campaign of their choice, concluded that the program boosted the number of candidates by 86%. Another study (https://web.stanford.edu/~neilm/The%20Impact%20of%20Public%20Financing%20on%20Electoral%20Competition.pdf) of Arizona and Maine’s programs found that they “significantly increased competition.”
Others disagreed. The United States Government Accountability Office, the nonpartisan research agency advising Congress, studied Arizona and Maine’s programs (https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-10-390.pdf) in 2010 and concluded there was no evidence that public financing led to more candidates.
There’s little evidence that public financing has curbed the influence of private donors, according to the Seattle study and the GAO report.
In California, few studies have examined the effectiveness of local programs. A 2023 San Francisco Ethics Commission study found candidates have increasingly tapped into the public funds and that third-party spending was “at near all-time lows.” But the commission encouraged a more comprehensive analysis. A 2013 study (https://www.oaklandca.gov/files/assets/city/v/3/boards-amp-commissions/documents/pec/publications/reports-by-third-parties/2013-05-01-evaluating-oaklands-limited-public-financing-act.pdf) in Oakland found no evidence its program diluted the influence of wealthy donors, although it did seem to boost competition.
Researchers point to the difficulty (https://sgp.jhu.edu/primers/public-funding-of-us-elections/#conclusion) of studying public financing programs, because most apply in only a handful of states and it is hard to measure what would have happened if the programs had not been in place.
The lack of compelling evidence makes Prop. 4 proponents’ claims shaky, the San Diego Union-Tribune’s editorial board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/04/endorsement-dont-buy-prop-4s-baloney-about-publicly-financed-campaigns/) argued.
“So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits,” it said.
The ballot measure should not be overly prescriptive, said Dora Rose, deputy director for the League of Women Voters of California, a co-sponsor of Prop. 4.
“Prop. 4 sets basic safeguards and then lets communities learn from the evidence and decide what works for them,” she said.
For now, voters appear skeptical. A September poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the Public Policy Institute of California found 53% of likely voters would oppose Prop. 4, while just 42% would vote yes. Another poll (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf) by the UC-Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies shows a tighter matchup, with 35% of likely voters supporting the measure and another 35% against it.

PROP 4: Repeal the Ban on Public Financing of Political Campaigns
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-09/California%20Decides_Proposition%204.pdf)
